title: Limit Cycles in a Photonic Dimer with Tuneable Non-Hermitian Interactions
authors: Kevin J. H. Peters, Peter Schnorrenberg, Daniel Ehrmanntraut, Nikolas Longen, Julian Schmitt
abstract: Interactions govern the emergence of collective behaviour in classical and quantum many-body systems. While conservative interactions are well known to generate nonlinear phenomena ranging from self-trapping to pattern formation, it remains largely unexplored whether purely dissipative -- i.e., non-Hermitian -- interactions can give rise to similarly rich dynamics and nontrivial system states. Here, we experimentally realise tuneable non-Hermitian interactions in two coupled condensates of light confined within a dye-filled double-well microcavity. Local coupling to molecular reservoirs generates the effective dissipative photon interactions. We show that the interplay between coherent tunnelling and interactions stabilises limit-cycle oscillations, a hallmark of nonlinear dynamics traditionally associated with Hermitian nonlinearities. By tuning the reservoir coupling, we map out the dynamical phase diagram comprising stable fixed points and limit cycles, thereby demonstrating direct control over the interaction strength. Our experimentally validated model reveals both supercritical and subcritical Hopf bifurcations, giving rise to hysteresis, bistability and excitability. These results validate dissipative interactions as a mechanism for organising collective nonlinear dynamics in driven-dissipative systems and pave the way towards exploring nonequilibrium many-body physics through controlled dissipation.
summary: This paper experimentally proves that purely dissipative, non-Hermitian interactions can generate rich nonlinear dynamics, like limit-cycle oscillations, in a photonic dimer system. By coupling the light fields to molecular reservoirs in a microcavity, the authors control the effective dissipation strength. This work validates controlled dissipation as a powerful mechanism for studying non-equilibrium many-body physics.
main_problem: The study investigates whether purely dissipative (non-Hermitian) interactions can generate rich nonlinear dynamics, such as limit-cycle oscillations, comparable to those from conservative interactions.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrate that limit-cycle oscillations, indicative of complex nonlinear dynamics, can be stabilized purely by tuning non-Hermitian interactions in a photonic dimer system.
method: The research combines theoretical modeling using Langevin equations and adiabatic elimination with experimental realization in a dye-filled double-well microcavity.
model_or_system: The system is a photonic dimer (two coupled condensates of light) in a microcavity, where effective dissipative interactions arise from local coupling to molecular reservoirs. The dynamics are governed by non-Hermitian terms derived from the reservoir coupling.
key_observables: Limit-cycle oscillations (LC), stable fixed points (FP), Hopf bifurcations, hysteresis, and excitability, observed via time traces and power spectral densities.
important_parameters: Tunable non-Hermitian interaction strength ($G_j$), pump rate ($\Gamma_{\uparrow 1}$), and cavity length ($D_0$) which sets the cutoff wavelength ($\lambda_c$).
main_assumptions: Adiabatic elimination of molecular dynamics ($\dot{m}_j \simeq 0$) is used to derive the effective non-Hermitian interaction term.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the model, the microcavity setup, the mapping of the dynamical phase diagram showing LC regions vs. fixed points, and time traces/histograms confirming the onset of limit cycles via Hopf bifurcations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by modeling the system with reservoir coupling, derives the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, and then presents experimental measurements mapping the dynamical phase diagram by tuning interaction strengths to observe bifurcations between stable fixed points and limit cycles.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete experimental platform demonstrating that non-Hermitian physics, traditionally associated with open quantum systems, can be a primary mechanism for organizing complex, nonlinear collective dynamics in quantum optics.
